title: Effect handlers: generators and one-shot continuations
body: An effect lets code ask its context to do something without knowing how. You declare one with `type _ Effect.t += Yield : int -> unit Effect.t`, and code performs it with `Effect.perform (Yield 3)`. A *handler* installed further up the stack decides what happens: it receives the request together with a continuation `k` that represents the rest of the suspended computation.

A continuation is *one-shot*: you must resume it exactly once, with `continue k v` to carry on or `discontinue k exn` to raise an exception at the suspension point. Resuming twice raises `Continuation_already_resumed`, and never resuming it leaks the suspended stack along with any resources it holds. When you stop early, `discontinue` is how the producer's `Fun.protect ~finally` and other cleanup run.

This is the mechanism behind schedulers, async IO libraries and generators. Handlers are written with `Effect.Deep.match_with`: `retc` handles a normal return, `exnc` handles an exception, and `effc` picks the effects you intercept (returning `None` forwards the rest to outer handlers). Keep handlers small and cancellation explicit.
challenge: src/gen.ml declares the `Yield` effect and `yield`, but `take` returns an empty list. Implement `take n producer` with a deep handler that collects up to n yielded values and then stops the producer by discontinuing its continuation with `Stop` so its cleanup runs. Define `to_list` as `take max_int`.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. Edit only src/gen.ml. The test includes an infinite producer and a producer with `Fun.protect ~finally`, so a leaked continuation shows up as a missing cleanup.
question: Why must `take` discontinue the continuation when it has enough values?
correct: A continuation must be resumed exactly once; discontinuing unwinds the producer so its cleanup code runs instead of leaking it
wrong: Continuations are garbage collected immediately, so it is optional
discontinue makes the producer run faster
reasoning: An unresumed continuation keeps its stack and resources alive; raising Stop inside it lets finally handlers run and releases them.
